query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The formation of a protective oxide layer through the addition of Cr to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance.
generation.intervention: Addition of Cr to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: High-temperature conditions (1000-1100°C) in an oxidizing atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer (Cr2O3 or CrTaO4-based oxide)
generation.mechanism: The protective oxide layer reduces oxygen permeability and prevents degradation of the alloy's mechanical properties
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature oxygen resistance, resulting in reduced mass gain and oxidation rate
generation.baseline: Untreated refractory high-entropy alloys with poor high-temperature oxygen resistance
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 1000-1100°C; Atmosphere: Oxidizing; Exposure conditions: Long-term exposure (up to 200 hours)
generation.uncertainty: Optimal composition and processing conditions for achieving a protective oxide layer are still unknown

falsification_experiment.design: Isothermal oxidation test at 1000°C for 200 hours
measurements: Microstructural analysis of the oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mass gain and oxidation rate of the Cr-added alloy are not significantly lower than those of the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract WVTaTiCr x ( x = 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) refractory high-entropy alloy coatings were prepared on a 42-CrMo steel plate using laser cladding. The purpose of this work is to investigate the effect of the Cr content on the microstructure and properties of the WVTaTiCr x coating. The morphologies and phase compositions of five coatings with different Cr contents were comparatively observed. In addition, the hardness and high-temperature oxidation resistance of the coatings were also analyzed. As a result, with the increase in Cr, the coating grains were more refined. All the coating is mainly composed of the BCC solid-solution phase, which promotes the precipitation of the Laves phase with the increase in Cr. The addition of Cr greatly improves the hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and corrosion resistance of the coating. The WVTaTiCr (Cr 1 ) exhibited superior mechanical properties, especially in terms of its exceptional hardness, high-temperature oxidation resistance and outstanding corrosion resistance. As the temperature capability of modern Ni- based superalloys has reached its limit for gas turbine engine applications, materials scientists are searching for new materials with higher temperature capabilities. Recently, “High-Entropy Alloy (HEA)” [1] , [2] has been proposed as a new strategy for alloy design with a wide composition space. Other names such as “compositionally complex alloys (CCAs)” has also been given to this class of alloy containing multiple phases [3] . Nevertheless, the alloy design strategy of HEA/CCA shows great promise for exploring new alloy systems. RHEA was first proposed by Senkov et al . [4] as an attempt to create new alloy systems for high temperature applications beyond superalloys. However, oxidation resistance is crucial since it could lead to severe degradation in mechanical properties. Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. decision.trend: Research has focused on improving the high-temperature oxidation resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys through various methods, including composition changes and surface engineering. The addition of Cr to WVTaTiCr x alloys has been shown to improve hardness and oxidation resistance. However, the optimal composition and processing conditions for achieving high-temperature oxygen resistance remain to be determined.
decision.unsolved: The development of refractory high-entropy alloys with improved high-temperature oxygen resistance for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions remains a challenge. Existing alloys often suffer from poor oxidation resistance, which can lead to degradation and failure.
decision.why: The formation of a protective oxide layer on the surface of the alloy could improve its high-temperature oxygen resistance. This could be achieved through the addition of elements that promote oxide layer formation, such as Cr or Al, or through surface engineering techniques like coating or nitriding. The optimal composition and processing conditions for achieving a protective oxide layer remain to be determined.
